v1.9.0 closes the 1.8 series. It is the release where the platform became something an organization
can run under its own governance — sign-in from their identity provider, accounts provisioned and
deactivated by it, passkeys as a second factor, and a deployment whose origins, billing posture and
region come from its own configuration rather than ours. Every identity surface ships dark behind a
flag; the OIDC and SCIM surfaces exist for dedicated deployments, and the managed platform does not
mount them. Around that, the series replaced the graph fleet's per-instance refresh with one command,
ran the first authenticated test of tenant isolation, and found — three times over — that an alarm can
sit green for the life of a stack while watching nothing at all.

Covers everything since v1.8.0; the 1.8.x patches carried generated changelogs.

## Identity for governed deployments

Account creation moved out of the register endpoint into a single provisioning kernel: one atomic
transaction across the user, its token, its personal organization and its limits, so a failure
part-way leaves no partial account where before several steps committed on their own. Register still
owns its gates — validation, CAPTCHA, rate limits — and now delegates the rest. That kernel is what
the two identity surfaces below build on.

**OIDC login.** A deployment can sign users in through its identity provider, behind
`SSO_OIDC_ENABLED`. Resolution is link-only, never just-in-time: an identity links once, by claim
equality against the identifier the provisioning path stamped, and is otherwise refused — so a
deactivated user is refused even with a valid token, and a deployment pinned to an enterprise
organization requires membership on every resolution, not only when the link is first made. The flow
carries single-use state, a browser-binding cookie, and ID-token validation against the issuer's own
keys; a deployment configured with no login method at all refuses to boot.

**SCIM 2.0.** Behind `SCIM_ENABLED`, an identity provider can create, read, update, deactivate and
list users against `/scim/v2`, authenticated by a per-organization provisioning token that no other
surface accepts and that expires by default. Deactivation delegates to the existing kill-switch —
session invalidation and API-key revocation — and reports whether every side effect took, answering
with a retryable failure when one did not rather than short-circuiting the provider's retry. Delete is
an idempotent deactivate, never destructive. Interoperability was corrected after the first review:
error envelopes are RFC 7644 at the top level of the body, and a profile replace applies email and
external-id changes, so an identity-provider-side email change before first sign-in no longer strands
the user.

**Posture, enforced.** `GET /v1/auth/providers` reports which methods a deployment offers — password,
OIDC, passkeys, registration — so one frontend build renders the right sign-in for each deployment.
The flags behind it are enforced at the endpoints, not merely advertised: with password authentication
disabled, every password-credential endpoint refuses, invitations included. Verification, reset and
invitation emails can target a designated login home with return context, which is what let
interactive sign-in consolidate onto one app during this series.

## Passkeys

The complete WebAuthn backend, behind `PASSKEYS_ENABLED`. After password verification an enrolled user
receives `status: mfa_required` and a short-lived, purpose-scoped token — refused as a session bearer —
redeemed at `/v1/auth/mfa/options` and `/verify` with an assertion or a recovery code. Enrollment
issues single-use recovery codes and a notification email; passwordless login uses discoverable
credentials; and with `MFA_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED`, an organization owner or admin signing in by
password without a passkey is routed through enrollment before a session is issued. Enrolling from
settings requires fresh proof — the current password or a re-authentication ceremony — mirroring what
removal already required, and the last passkey of an enforced role cannot be removed. Token
redemption, attempt budgets and recovery-code consumption are single atomic claims that fail closed.

`AuthResponse` gains `status` and `mfa_token`, both additive with defaults, so the register and SSO
contracts are unchanged and the login path is byte-identical with the flag off. The surface was
hardened after an internal review before being enabled anywhere.

## Running it somewhere else

Three things a dedicated deployment needed that the managed platform never had to ask for. **CORS
origins derive from the deployment's own app URLs**, so frontend origins, OAuth redirect validation and
the MCP remote origin check all follow wherever the apps are served — the managed lists are reproduced
byte-for-byte and pinned by test. **A billing-disabled deployment behaves like one**: the billing
portal answers `billing_disabled: true` instead of failing against a payment provider it has no
credentials for, and subscription and overage invoices still generate as the usage record but at zero
amounts, since the fee is settled off-platform. **Bootstrap keeps its region**: the setup script was
resetting `AWS_REGION` to a hardcoded default after the bootstrap had threaded the real one everywhere
else, so a fork outside that region lost it on the way out.

## Provenance of what reaches production

All 105 action references across 27 workflows are pinned to commit SHAs — among them the step that
assumes the deploy role — with the version kept in a trailing comment.
`CONTRIBUTING.md` gained the fork path, a licensing statement (Apache 2.0 inbound equals outbound, no
CLA) and a per-pull-request certification of provenance; fork pull requests are pinned to
GitHub-hosted runners regardless of how the runner variable is later set. Release deployments are
dispatch-only, and prod dispatch now requires the tag job to have succeeded rather than being reachable
after a failed one. `actionlint` joined the code-quality gate after a workflow that would not parse
reached `main` past a hand-written check that could not see the class of error.

## The graph fleet, as one command

The container refresh no longer enumerates instances into a GitHub Actions matrix with a runner job
apiece — a hard ceiling that a fleet of dedicated instances would eventually have hit. It runs as a
script on the instance, and the pipeline issues **one tag-targeted SSM command per node-type group**
through a small Lambda that dispatches and aggregates without waiting. Failures page through
EventBridge whether or not anyone is watching the run; a not-yet-cycled instance reports a skip rather
than a failure; a rate-control budget halts a genuinely bad rollout; and a forced restart exists for
the one case that needs it — monthly credential rotation, where the image is unchanged and the restart
is the work.

Writing down what a refresh actually needs surfaced six live defects in the old path, all the same
shape — a fact held in two places that had drifted. Two were silent: replicas restarting without their
mounts because nine variables were exported at boot and persisted nowhere, and a refresh pulling the
environment tag rather than the tag the instance had been pinned to, which defeated the pin during the
exact engine-upgrade window it protects. The first production run of the new path found three more of
its own, fixed the same night. AMI delivery through the maintenance workflow now dispatches a real
deploy, since an instance refresh cannot move the AMI into the launch template it boots from.

## Tenant isolation, tested

A black-box harness provisions two independent tenants against a live deployment and fires a
cross-tenant and privilege-escalation matrix at it — REST reads, Cypher, destructive graph operations,
MCP tools, GraphQL, and both extension command surfaces, in both directions — classifying each answer
against the owner's own response rather than by status code alone. It is the first authenticated test
of the product's load-bearing claim. Run against a full local deployment, every cross-tenant probe was
denied. The harness is opt-in and
gates nothing in the ordinary suite; the one production-code change it needed is a test-support flag
that cannot take effect in production.

Also on the access surface: a graph-scoped API key is now accepted on its own graph's GraphQL
endpoint, as it already was on that graph's operations and MCP surfaces — the URL is the scope. It
remains rejected everywhere else.

## Alarms that watched nothing

The series found three instances of one trap: an alarm whose metric dimensions are a subset of what
the agent publishes matches **no stream at all**, and reads `OK` on *no datapoints received* for the
life of the stack. The graph disk-usage alarms had done so since creation. `AllocationFailures` — the
alarm that reports a paying customer's graph creation failing for lack of capacity — had a second
problem underneath the first: the worker's IAM grant permitted a different metric namespace, so every
publish was denied and swallowed, since February. The notification-delivery alarm added in v1.8.0 had
never been accepted by CloudWatch at all. All are corrected, the disk and delivery alarms as Metrics
Insights queries, which aggregate across dimension sets and pick up new resources without anyone
remembering to add them.

Also: `api.yaml` deploys from S3 rather than inline, which frees it from a size ceiling it was ten
lines under and lets its alarms live beside the resources they watch instead of in the account-global
security stack; the refresh dispatcher has an errors alarm; and RDS gains a connection-count alarm
whose threshold follows the instance class.

Three more places that detected a condition and told nobody now page. The shared master's serving
container being killed and restarted under the nightly materialization — which happened twice in one
week and was caught only by a red orchestration run — has its own alarm, tuned so the master's
deliberate nightly wake is one start and does not page while a second start within twelve hours does.
The daily graph-registry sweep no longer **deletes** a registry row whose instance is missing from the
instance registry: that row is a live graph's routing, and the instance registry drifts on fleet
cycling, so a slow volume re-attach was turning a transient drift into a permanent orphan. The sweep
marks such rows, clears the mark when the instance returns, publishes the count, and an alarm watches
it. And the reaper that writes off a subscription whose provisioning never finished — a customer who
paid and has no resource — now pages on every occurrence instead of leaving one error line in a log.

## Billing: what production actually does

Walking the paid signup path end to end on production found what reading it had not. A cold checkout
could collect payment and provision the graph, yet leave the subscription stranded at `provisioning` —
the long graph build invalidated the session holding the subscription, so the link never persisted and
activation failed. Completion now runs in a fresh session with no awaits interleaved. A webhook
redelivery was overwriting the checkout session id the status page polls, leaving the customer on a
permanent 404 after paying. And an immediate "delete now" was being silently undone: the provider's
`subscription.deleted` webhook pushed the end date back out to the period end, so the graph never
suspended and kept running — and billing — to the end of the period.

Offboarding now deletes a graph's documents and purges its search-index content, which a soft-deleted
graph row had been quietly keeping alive; the organization graph limit is applied at checkout as it
already was at creation. Dead overage-invoice scaffolding for a postpaid model the platform does not
have was removed, three declared-but-never-written records now get written — including payment audit
events, which are compliance evidence — and the higher-volume usage table gained the retention policy
its sibling already had, landing before there was any data a mistake could destroy.

Two more refuse-the-sale gates and one compensator proven. A graph checkout now checks writer capacity
for the tier before the payment session, exactly as it already checked the organization's graph limit,
and fails closed when capacity cannot be determined — provisioning runs after payment, so a sale that
completes against a full fleet is money taken for a graph that cannot be delivered. The rollback for a
paid tier upgrade, whose four tests had all patched it out, now executes for real in the
reattachment-timeout case and every post-condition holds: the volume re-attached to the old instance,
its registry tier reverted, the graph registry taken off `migrating`, and the subscription back at the
old plan and price. And the provisioning-claim suite, which proved the mutex against real threads and
a real database, now also pins the second half of the double-provisioning blast radius — one credit
pool per graph, refused by the database itself if anything got past the claim.

## Taxonomy

The rs-gaap rollup rules were rebuilt from the live calculation arcs. Their generator had been unable
to run since the per-subtotal networks were collapsed in June, and a later leaf split then left six
rules enumerating concepts the calculation graph no longer arcs — not inert, since a rule whose parent
has no live children falls back to its frozen enumeration and reports a false failure against a real
subtotal. The generator is retired in favor of a drift gate that holds the rules against the source. A
second migration then repaired the key spelling the first had written, which had every rollup
evaluation recording an error rather than a verdict; both migrations fan into every tenant schema.

## Fixes

- **The published file-size limit is the enforced one.** `/limits` and `/tiers` advertised 1, 5 and
  10 GB per tier while the write path refused anything over 100 MB — a customer told 10 GB received a
  400 at 100 MB. The published figure is now derived from the enforced constant, so every tier reads
  the same, much smaller, number; nothing could exceed it before. `FileUploadRequest` accepts an
  optional `file_size_bytes` so an over-limit upload is refused at presign rather than after the push.
- **SEC statement reads no longer collapse a Q4 and an FY fact** that share a concept and an end date;
  the survivor was arbitrary and unstable between identical calls. `financial-statement-analysis` can
  now legitimately return both rows.
- The SEC nightly materialization runs as a full rebuild — incremental mode exceeded the shared
  master's memory at the current corpus size — and a per-database run limit ensures two
  materializations can never write the same graph concurrently.
- The SEC connector's instructions no longer direct users to a historical subgraph with no serving path.
- **Capacity warnings reach every graph admin.** The storage-usage sensor picked one arbitrary
  explicit graph admin for both the storage snapshot and the 80%/100% email, so an organization-owned
  graph whose only admins were the organization's owner and admins — implicit, with no explicit grant
  row — wrote no snapshot and sent no warning at all. Recipients now resolve to explicit graph admins
  plus the organization's owners and admins; the snapshot is attributed to the monitor, not a member.
- `GET /v1/graphs/{id}/metrics` refuses shared repositories up front instead of issuing a full-scan
  count per label and per relationship type against the shared master; the only consumer already
  skipped repositories because the call timed out.
- An authentication-cache invalidation path was corrected and gained the tests it did not have.
- Fork-safe demo runners: the roboledger and roboinvestor demos honor `DEMO_API_URL`, keep credentials
  per target, and are strictly API-only against anything but the local stack; the scenario runner can
  skip the report-serialization pass.
- Twenty-one documentation files were realigned with the code, and CloudFormation's README — 62 commits
  behind — now points at authoritative sources instead of restating values that rot.

## API surface changes

No endpoint or field was removed in this series. Additions ride the SDK's generated tier and are already
in the published clients (1.10.1):

- New, schema-visible: `GET /v1/auth/providers`; `/v1/auth/passkeys/*` (register, login, re-auth,
  list, remove); `/v1/auth/mfa/*` (options, verify, status, recovery-code regeneration).
- New, schema-excluded by design: the OIDC redirect endpoints and `/scim/v2`.
- Additive fields: `AuthResponse.status` / `mfa_token`; `PortalSessionResponse.billing_disabled`;
  `OrgInvitationResponse.token` (null everywhere except a non-production build with the test-support
  flag on); `FileUploadRequest.file_size_bytes` — this last is stable-tier surface the integration
  template imports, and is optional with a default, so no coordinated client major.
- A published value changes: `max_file_size_gb` on `/limits` and `/tiers` is now the same figure on
  every tier. Any material quoting the old per-tier values is now wrong.
- Response content, not shape: `financial-statement-analysis` may return two rows where it returned one.
- Status change: `GET /v1/graphs/{id}/metrics` on a shared repository returns 400 (it previously
  timed out or returned 404); `POST /v1/billing/checkout` for a graph tier with no free writer slot
  returns 409 before any payment session is created.

## Deploying this release

- **Migrations on both databases**, all run automatically when the new Dagster daemon boots.
  Platform: `password_hash` nullable with an indexed `external_id`; the `user_identities` and
  `scim_tokens` tables; the `user_passkeys` and `user_mfa_recovery_codes` tables. Extensions: the
  rs-gaap rollup repair (0030) and the rule-variable key spelling (0031), both of which rewrite rule rows
  in `public` and every tenant schema. Until 0031 has run, rollup verification records `error` on
  every evaluation; nothing else in the release depends on the new tables.
- **CloudFormation stack updates**: `api` (now uploaded to the deployment bucket and deployed by URL),
  `security`, `graph-infra`, `graph-volumes`, `graph-ladybug-replicas`, `postgres`, `worker`, and
  `dagster` (the stalled-provisioning write-off alarm). The
  API alarms move from `security` into `api` under the same names within a single run; deploying prod
  first keeps that gap to the minutes between the two jobs.
- **The shared-replica root-volume alarm may read `ALARM` on first deploy** if the fleet is near the
  threshold. It is a real signal, cleared by raising `SHARED_REPLICAS_ROOT_VOLUME_SIZE_<ENV>` — a
  launch-template property, so the same deploy cycles the replica fleet onto the larger volume.
- Every identity flag — `SSO_OIDC_ENABLED`, `SCIM_ENABLED`, `PASSKEYS_ENABLED`,
  `MFA_ENFORCEMENT_ENABLED`, `ENTERPRISE_ORG_ID` — defaults off. Enabling the SSO surface is a
  sequence, not a flip: bootstrap the enterprise organization, pin it, restart. Boot validation refuses
  a deployment that enables the surface without rate limiting or leaves itself no login method.
